<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Emergency undocking in robotic surgery is an uncommon but high-stakes event. Published protocols are predominantly single-institution and specialty-specific, and no multidisciplinary cross-specialty consensus exists. This study aimed to establish expert consensus on the definitions and procedural steps of safe emergency undocking. A four-round modified Delphi study was conducted with an international panel of robotic theatre team members. Round 1 used open-text questions to generate themes; Rounds 2 to 4 presented binary statements (Yes / No / Unable to rate), with a pre-specified threshold of 80% agreement and Unable to rate responses excluded from the denominator. Items below threshold, or reaching threshold with substantive comments, were revised and re-presented. Fifty-two experts from 10 countries consented and completed Round 1. The panel comprised lead or experienced console surgeons (53.8%), first assistants (30.8%), surgical care practitioners (9.6%), anaesthetists (3.8%), and one industry representative (1.9%). Response rates were 80.8%, 80.8%, and 76.9% for Rounds 2 to 4 respectively. Thirty-seven statements reached consensus, comprising two definitions, six common pathway items, 18 controlled undocking items, and 11 uncontrolled undocking items. Of the 37 statements, 25 were classified as platform-agnostic and 12 as platform-dependent. Three role-allocation items were deferred to a planned subsequent round. This Delphi process produced 37 consensus statements defining controlled and uncontrolled emergency undocking and the steps for each. The panel was predominantly United Kingdom-based and surgical, and included no scrub or circulating practitioners. The resulting framework requires simulation and clinical validation before implementation.</jats:p>
title: Emergency undocking in robotic surgery: an international Delphi consensus study

assertion.value: This study involved healthcare professionals providing expert opinion on clinical protocol content. No patients, patient data, or patient-identifiable information were involved and no clinical intervention was undertaken. Formal research ethics committee approval was therefore not required. All participants provided electronic informed consent prior to Round 1, recorded for all 52 panellists.
